summary: This document extends LDP to create label switched paths for Maximally Redundant Trees, used mainly for IP/LDP Fast Reroute (MRT-FRR). The only protocol extension needed is the ability to advertise an MRT Capability.

plainLanguage.summary: MRTs are two backup routes that share as little as possible. This adds a way for routers to tell each other about them so a failure can be detoured around.

questions: what is the ldp mrt capability tlv
what is the rainbow fec in ldp
subtitle: How LDP routers tell each other they support Maximally Redundant Trees, so backup label paths exist before a failure.

tldr.problem: IP/LDP Fast Reroute with Maximally Redundant Trees (MRT-FRR) needs two extra sets of label switched paths, one per tree, built ahead of time so a router can switch the moment a link or node fails.
tldr.mechanism: LDP gains one new capability, the MRT Capability TLV. Routers that negotiate it advertise labels for MRT-Red and MRT-Blue forwarding topologies using multi-topology IDs, plus a Rainbow ID that lets one label cover all topologies.
tldr.outcome: LDP can carry the labels MRT-FRR needs. Alternate paths do not follow shortest paths, so network security must not assume that malicious traffic only follows shortest paths.

today: RFC 8320 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2018. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC in the metadata, and it works together with the MRT architecture in RFC 7812.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8320 describes the LDP signaling and behavior needed by the architecture for IP/LDP Fast Reroute using Maximally Redundant Trees (MRTs), which is specified in RFC 7812. For each destination, MRT-FRR creates two alternate destination-based trees, separate from the shortest-path forwarding used in stable operation. LDP signals Forwarding Equivalency Classes (FECs) for these two sets of trees, called MRT-Blue and MRT-Red, using the multi-topology extensions of RFC 7307.

LDP depends on an IGP for the computation of MRTs and alternates, and all routers must run at least one common standardized algorithm, such as the MRT Lowpoint algorithm in RFC 7811. MRT-FRR can provide 100% coverage for link and node failures in an arbitrary topology where the failure does not partition the network, and it can be deployed incrementally as an MRT Island of connected supporting routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is a ready-made detour for every road. Routers need a way to share the detour signs ahead of time, and this RFC adds that.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
Redundant Trees are a pair of trees where the path from any node X to the root R along the first tree is node-disjoint with the path from X to the root along the second. Maximally Redundant Trees share the minimum possible number of nodes and links. In graphs that are not 2-connected, redundant trees cannot be computed, but MRTs can, and they are as redundant as the network graph allows.

  • MRT-Red and MRT-Blue: the two MRTs, each with an associated forwarding topology and MPLS MT-ID.
  • Rainbow MRT: an MPLS MT-ID that refers to the multiple MRT forwarding topologies and the default topology, used to reduce signaling.
  • MRT Island: the routers supporting a particular MRT Profile and the links connecting them.
  • Island Border Router (IBR): an Island router connected to a router outside the Island in the same area or level. That outside router is an Island Neighbor (IN).
sections.plainLanguage: Two routes that overlap as little as possible are "red" and "blue". The "rainbow" is a shortcut sign that means all of them at once.

sections.title: Advertising the MRT Capability
sections.content:
Routers must know which LDP neighbors support MRT. A new MRT Capability Parameter TLV is defined following the LDP capability guidelines of RFC 5561. It can be sent during session initialization or after the session is established. If a router advertises the capability but its peer has not, the router MUST NOT advertise MRT-related FEC-label bindings to that peer.

Supporting MRT means sending and receiving multi-topology FEC elements, understanding the Rainbow MRT MT-ID, advertising the Rainbow FEC to the right neighbors, acting as egress for MRT-Red and MRT-Blue when acting as egress for a prefix in the default topology, and originating MRT-Red and MRT-Blue FECs for a prefix learned from a neighbor that does not support MRT.

An LSR advertising the MRT Capability MUST also advertise the LDP Multi-Topology (MT) Capability. If MRT is negotiated without MT, the LSR behaves as if MRT was not negotiated and answers with the status code "MRT Capability negotiated without MT Capability" in an advisory Notification (E-bit 0); the session SHOULD NOT be terminated. The capability does not distinguish IPv4 from IPv6: a router is expected to advertise MRT bindings for the same address families as its shortest-path bindings, and advertising for only one of two is not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the detour signs, routers check that their neighbor also knows about them. If the neighbor does not, they keep the detour signs to themselves.

sections.title: The MRT Capability TLV
sections.content: The TLV has type 0x050E and a length of 1 octet. The U-bit MUST be 1, so a router that does not recognize the TLV silently ignores it and processes the rest of the message. The F-bit MUST be 0, as required by Section 3 of RFC 5561. The one-octet value holds the S-bit followed by reserved bits. The S-bit MUST be 1 in an LDP Initialization message; in the dynamic Capability message it may be 1 to advertise or 0 to withdraw the capability.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a tiny form with one tick box that says "yes, I understand the detour signs".

sections.title: MRT FECs and the Rainbow FEC
sections.content:
MRT uses the MT Prefix FEC encoding of RFC 7307 unchanged for MRT-Blue, MRT-Red and Rainbow MRT FECs. The Default MRT Profile uses MPLS MT-ID 3946 for MRT-Red and 3947 for MRT-Blue, and the Rainbow MRT MT-ID is 3945. LDP must use the same label distribution control, label retention and label advertisement modes for shortest-path FECs and MRT FECs, because the paths must exist before a failure so the point of local repair can use them at once.

An Area Border Router (ABR) needs different neighbors to use different labels when sending to it for the same FEC. To peers in the same area as the best route, the ABR advertises two labels, one for MRT-Red and one for MRT-Blue (best-area behavior). To all other MRT peers it advertises one binding in the Rainbow MRT MT-ID using the label of the default tree, used for both red and blue traffic (non-best-area behavior). The Rainbow FEC is RECOMMENDED for non-best-area advertisements. The Rainbow MT-ID can also carry an IMPLICIT_NULL or EXPLICIT_NULL label that applies to all three FEC types, which is generally useful only when the FEC refers to the LSR itself.

When switching behavior for a destination, the ABR MUST withdraw the old mappings and then advertise the new ones. If a receiver sees conflicting advertisements, it keeps the mapping it already has and sends a Label Release for the new one. A neighbor that receives a Rainbow FEC mapping MUST NOT propagate it.
sections.plainLanguage: A busy intersection hands out two special signs, red and blue, to neighbors on the main side. Everyone else gets one all-purpose rainbow sign that works for both.

sections.title: Applying LDP Rules to Red and Blue FECs
sections.content:
The procedures of RFC 5036 apply to red and blue FECs once reinterpreted. An LDP peer means a peer that negotiated the MRT Capability. The next hop of a red or blue FEC is based on the MRT-Red or MRT-Blue tree. A red(blue) proxy-node attachment router for a multi-homed prefix MUST originate the label mapping for the red(blue) FEC. If it is an IBR, it forwards packets to the Island Neighbor by swapping to the shortest-path label, or popping the label if the neighbor does not support LDP.

An LSR may be egress for a red(blue) FEC when the prefix refers to the LSR itself, when it is the proxy-node attachment router, or when it is an ABR and the peer needs non-best-area behavior. A proxy-node attachment router should generally not advertise an implicit or explicit null label for a red or blue FEC, since it needs to receive that traffic with a non-null label to forward it correctly. A Rainbow FEC mapping from an ABR satisfies label-existence checks for the matching red and blue FECs, and a red or blue FEC matches the routing table if the shortest-path FEC does.

The MRT topology comes from IGP advertisements, so missing MRT LDP advertisements do not change it; they leave gaps in forwarding entries. MRT is designed to work with LDP IGP Synchronization (RFC 5443): a link advertised at maximum cost is excluded from the MRT Island.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook is reused, but "the next road" now means the next road on the red or blue detour. Special rules say who hands out the final sign at the end of each detour.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The labels distributed here create forwarding paths that do not follow shortest-path routes, and the swapping operations are created in normal operation, before any failure. A malicious packet with an appropriate label injected from a compromised location would therefore be forwarded along a non-shortest path. A network security design should not assume that malicious traffic only follows shortest paths. The RFC notes this is not unique to MRT, since RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) can also build non-shortest paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Detour signs are put up all the time, not only during a blockage. Someone sneaky with the right sign could be sent down a detour, so guards should not assume everyone takes the main road.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and MT-ID Ranges
sections.content:
IANA allocated the MRT Capability TLV (0x050E) and the LDP status code "MRT Capability negotiated without MT Capability" (0x00000034, E-bit 0). From the MPLS Multi-Topology Identifiers registry it allocated 3945 (Rainbow MRT), 3946 (Default Profile MRT-Red) and 3947 (Default Profile MRT-Blue), and marked 3948-3995 as unassigned for future MRT-related values.

The values fall within 1 through 4095 so the same number can serve as a PIM MT-ID, whose range RFC 6420 limits to that span. This leaves 51 MRT-related values, enough for 25 MRT Profiles with red and blue pairs plus the Rainbow value.
sections.plainLanguage: Official numbers were reserved for the new signs, with spare numbers kept for future detour styles.
